author: Athul Prem

measured_linux_map_execution.scope: GNU time measurement for the native Linux map invocation, including assembly and solve.

transmission_eigenchannel_method.description: Squared singular values of the native transmission matrix give the eigenvalues of the transmitted-power operator T^H T at the original planes. Each eigenvalue is the transmitted fraction for a corresponding unit-power coherent input. They are ranked from largest to smallest without native mode labels. The trace is the sum for five separate 1 W drives. Trace divided by five gives the transmission fraction for equal mutually incoherent input power.
transmission_eigenchannel_method.unitary_bounds: The maximum change in ranked eigenvalues lower-bounds the operator norm of the transmitted-power difference under any unitary input basis change. The maximum change in ranked singular values gives the corresponding bound for the amplitude matrix under arbitrary unitary input and output basis changes. A nonzero spectral change rules out unitary port mixing alone for that finite comparison.

central_layer_control.scope: The four finite corners retain the original physical planes and a common signed mode anchor. The 168.75 nm two-layer case reuses Windows preparation with a Linux solve. The other three cases use native Linux preparation and solving. The interaction measures central and layer sensitivity on these footprints, including compatible port resolution and the disclosed preparation differences. Continuum and frequency convergence remain unresolved.

scope: Signed lab displacement modes are matched by mass-weighted overlap on the richer section. Each end uses the same native section with its verified body trace. T and R sum the original propagating modal powers for the matched left input. The saved independent flux receipts check all five inputs and their coherent superpositions. Complex changes align mode gauges at the original end planes. Body layers and compatible port discretization change together on each fixed footprint. Finite comparisons at 1 GHz leave continuum and frequency convergence unresolved.
